text: After feature engineering you may have dozens or hundreds of columns. It's tempting to throw them all at the model and let it sort things out. Sometimes that works, but more features also mean more noise to overfit, slower training, harder explanations, and more data to collect and maintain in production. Feature selection is the discipline of keeping the features that earn their place.

Why drop features at all? Overfitting — irrelevant columns give the model extra ways to memorize noise. Speed and cost — fewer columns train and predict faster, and cost less to store. Interpretability — explaining a model with 8 inputs is far easier than one with 800. And robustness — every feature is a data pipeline that can break in production. Selection isn't free, though — it can discard a feature that only helps in combination with others.

Three families of methods. Filter methods score each feature on its own using a statistic, then keep the top scorers — fast and model-agnostic. Wrapper methods repeatedly train a model on different feature subsets and keep whichever performs best — slower, but they consider features working together. Embedded methods select as part of training itself, like Lasso regression shrinking unhelpful coefficients to exactly zero.

scikit-learn's bundled diabetes dataset has 442 patients, 10 numeric features, and a disease-progression target. VarianceThreshold at 0.0 drops columns that never change — here all 10 survive. SelectKBest with an F-test ranks each feature by how strongly it relates to the target: bmi scores 230.7 and s5 scores 207.3, the highest, while sex barely registers at 0.8.

Keeping the top 4 by that filter gives bmi, bp, s4, and s5. Now the wrapper approach — recursive feature elimination trains the model, discards the weakest feature, and repeats until four remain. It picks a different set: bmi, s1, s2, and s5.

Notice s1 and s2 are strongly related to each other, so the wrapper judges them jointly, while the filter scored each alone. Different methods can disagree, and that's completely normal — they're answering slightly different questions.

Selecting features using the whole dataset, then splitting for validation, leaks information from the test rows into your choices. The fix is to put the selector inside a pipeline, so it's refit on the training portion of every single fold.

The 5-fold mean R-squared comes out to 0.46 for just four selected features, versus 0.482 for plain linear regression using all ten. Four features recover most of the performance — a useful trade when simplicity matters, though don't assume that's always true. The evidence, not a rule, decides.

To recap: feature selection keeps the inputs that earn their place. Filters are fast, wrappers consider combinations, and embedded methods select while training. Always fit selectors on training data only, ideally inside a pipeline, and judge them by validated performance. Next we begin the core algorithms, starting with linear regression.
